name: llamafile
license: Apache-2.0 for the project; its changes to llama.cpp and whisper.cpp are MIT, per the repo README
notable_features: Model weights are appended to the executable: one file is both the runtime and the model, and it maps itself into memory (an `ape` loader is extracted to $TMPDIR on UNIX).
Ships as a family of *files*: the same single-file idea applied to whisper.cpp (whisperfile) and stable-diffusion.cpp (diffusionfile), so an app can ship LLM + ASR + image gen with no installer.

GPU DSOs (ggml-cuda / ggml-rocm / ggml-vulkan) are loaded at runtime from the executable's directory first, then the bundle, then ~/.llamafile/v/<version>, then $HOME — so a hand-built DSO overrides the shipped one.
On macOS it compiles a small Metal module on first run using the Xcode Command Line Tools instead of shipping a prebuilt one.
Silently falls back to CPU inference if no GPU backend can be set up; `--gpu nvidia|amd|vulkan` forces a backend and turns that quiet fallback into a startup error.
Also ships Whisperfile, the same trick applied to speech-to-text.
hardware_caveats: AMD64 CPUs must have AVX or llamafile prints an error and refuses to run; AVX512, AVX2, FMA, F16C and VNNI are enabled conditionally at runtime. ARM64 requires ARMv8a, which covers Apple Silicon and 64-bit Raspberry Pi.
There is NO Intel oneAPI/SYCL backend. Per the support docs, Vulkan is what covers Intel and other hardware that CUDA and ROCm do not.
Zen4 is called out specifically: its AVX512 is very good and speeds up bf16 llamafiles. So on AMD the ISA generation, not just vendor, decides CPU throughput.

NVIDIA and AMD owners must pass `-ngl 999` to enable offloading; Metal offloads by default. Multiple GPUs are split evenly, and multi-GPU is documented as possibly broken on Radeon (workaround: HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0).

The bundled CUDA library is size-optimized and OMITS the IQ-quant kernels (IQ1_*, IQ2_*, IQ3_*, IQ4_*). Offloading an IQ-quant model to NVIDIA therefore leaves just those layers on the CPU — output is correct, those layers just get no acceleration. The Metal and ROCm builds are not size-optimized and do include full IQ-quant GPU support.
On Windows only executables under 4GB can run, so any self-contained llamafile above 4GB will not work; use the binary with external GGUF weights, or run under WSL (which also lifts the 4GB limit).
Vulkan on macOS goes through MoltenVK; the docs say Apple Silicon users normally want the built-in Metal backend instead.
CUDA via cuBLAS on Windows requires building from an x64 MSVC command prompt; release binaries ship prebuilt DLLs and are the recommended path.
best_for: Handing someone a model with zero install friction: email one file, they double-click it.
Air-gapped, edge, kiosk, or locked-down machines where you cannot install a Python or CUDA stack.
Ship a complete local AI app (LLM + speech-to-text + image gen) as portable executables per platform.
Getting a consumer GPU working without CUDA: Intel Arc and anything else ROCm does not cover run via the bundled Vulkan path.
Single-user laptop chat where simplicity beats tuning.
avoid_for: Multi-user or throughput serving — scheduling is none, one model per process.
Squeezing maximum tok/s out of a CUDA or ROCm box; the bundled CUDA DSO is size-optimized and drops IQ-quant kernels, and upstream llama.cpp/forks are faster.
Anyone needing Intel oneAPI/SYCL, DirectML, or OpenVINO paths.
Production serving where you need paged KV, continuous batching, or a scheduler.
Bundling models over 4GB into a Windows executable.
notes: Record focuses on llamafile as a distribution/packaging engine; the underlying llama.cpp kernels and ggml backend list belong to the llama.cpp record. Two version-sensitive claims worth re-checking on upgrade: (a) the IQ-quant exclusion applies to the size-optimized NVIDIA CUDA DSO shipped in releases — the docs say the Metal and ROCm builds are not size-optimized, and building a full CUDA library restores IQ acceleration; (b) the 0.10.x series is explicitly described by the project as not yet tested on every GPU and platform, with the AMD and Windows paths called best-effort. The support page was last updated roughly 2 months before access. I did not attempt to source a quantitative Vulkan-vs-native-backend performance gap; no primary source was found, so no such number is recorded here.
